source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate among LLM agents often lowers accuracy compared with majority vote taken before any debate. On CommonsenseQA debate harmed accuracy in every group mix tested.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; 100 questions x 5 seeds per cell; CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K. Worst MMLU drop in a mixed 3-agent group: 40.0 to 28.0 (-12.0 points). Another mixed group: 51.8 to 43.6 (-8.2) on MMLU and 58.2 to 50.2 (-8.0) on CSQA. Some groups gained (e.g. 66.2 to 68.0 on MMLU, 88.4 to 92.8 on GSM8K).
limits: Small models, 100 items per cell, 3 agents, 3 tasks. Table symbols were garbled in the PDF text, so which group is which row is not certain. Effects vary by task; GSM8K often improves.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that letting sampled drafts see each other helps. Compare against a no-exchange vote baseline (G9).

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Over rounds, correct-to-incorrect answer flips outnumber incorrect-to-correct flips. Resistance to flipping falls in round 2 versus round 1.
numbers: Aggregated over rounds in Fig 2-3 of paper; flip probability rises with the number of other agents who disagree (Fig 4). Exact percentages only in figures.
limits: Numbers are in figures, not text. Same small-model setup.
agent_relevance: Premature agreement shows up as a measurable flip of correct drafts under peer pressure. Track a draft that was right and then changed.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Adding a weaker model to a debate with stronger models can pull the group below the no-debate vote, even when strong models are the majority.
numbers: Configs such as 2 GPT-4o-mini + 1 Mistral and 1 GPT + 2 Mistral tested; text states debate harmed stronger-majority groups on CSQA and MMLU. Example: 2 weaker + 1 stronger CSQA 58.2 to 50.2.
limits: Only three model families.
agent_relevance: Mixing in a low-quality critic or sample can hurt. Gate peer input by track record, not by count.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: A prompt telling agents to maximise a correctness payoff did not reduce correct-to-incorrect flips. Prompting alone does not fix agreement bias.
numbers: Correctness-payoff system prompt tested on 3 models x 3 tasks (Fig 5); text says no apparent decrease in bad flips.
limits: Single prompt design; figure-level evidence.
agent_relevance: An instruction to be accurate is not a structural guard. Needs a structure like an independent first answer (G9 design).

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs? (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Majority voting over independent first answers captures most of the gain usually credited to multi-agent debate.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 5 agents, 7 benchmarks, average accuracy: single agent 0.7205; majority vote 0.7691; decentralized debate T=2 0.7377, T=3 0.7112, T=5 0.7050; sparse debate T=2 0.7330; centralized debate T=2 0.6551. Arithmetic: vote 0.99 vs decentralized T=5 0.67. Llama3.1-8B: vote average 0.7242.
limits: Small open models; 5 agents; debate beats single agent but not vote. Qwen2.5-32B shows same pattern per paper.
agent_relevance: Strong support for keeping drafts independent and aggregating, rather than letting them converge by talk.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs? (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Theory: if agents update beliefs by seeing peers, belief in the correct answer is a martingale. Debate alone gives no expected gain in correctness.
numbers: Theorem 2 (martingale under Dirichlet-compound-multinomial belief model); empirical belief curves flat across rounds.
limits: Holds for homogeneous or clique-structured topologies; heterogeneous fully connected debate need not be a martingale (paper Appendix).
agent_relevance: Explains why talk adds no expected accuracy; gains must come from an asymmetric update (verification), not from agreeing.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs? (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Biasing the update toward correct answers helps a lot. An oracle that locks in correct answers lifts accuracy; majority-based rules lift less but beat vanilla debate.
numbers: Decentralized T=5 MMLU formal logic 0.5000 to 0.6825 with oracle. Qwen average at T=5 (as read from Table 2, rows partly garbled): vanilla 0.7160, Conformist 0.7439, Follower (30% adopt majority) 0.7527, oracle 0.8364. HH-RLHF vanilla 0.4833 vs oracle 0.6600.
limits: Oracle needs ground truth, so it is an upper bound. Conformist rule keeps an answer that matches majority: that is conformity helping when the majority is usually right.
agent_relevance: A verifier that can mark a draft as checked-correct and freeze it is the practical analogue. Conformity helps only when the majority is more reliable than the individual.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs (ICML 2024)
finding: Across medical and other QA sets, debate protocols do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling, and are sensitive to hyperparameters.
numbers: Protocols tested: Multi-Persona, ChatEval, Society of Mind and others vs self-consistency and Medprompt. Authors report debate not reliably better; extra compute past a point does not guarantee gain.
limits: Tuned MAD can win. Tuning results are on a 376-question USMLE subset.
agent_relevance: Debate depends on settings; reports of gains may not be robust.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs (ICML 2024)
finding: Rival result: prompting agents to AGREE more (agreement intensity) raised accuracy on medical QA. Multi-Persona went from worst to best protocol.
numbers: Prompt: agree with the other agents X% of the time; X from 0 to 100% on 376 USMLE questions: about +15% for Multi-Persona, +5% for Society of Mind, ChatEval barely changed; 90% agreement used on full MedQA. On the counter-intuitive CIAR data the reverse held: more disagreement helped.
limits: Dataset dependent: MedQA and PubMedQA liked high agreement, CIAR liked disagreement.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: agreement is not always premature. Optimal consensus level depends on whether first instincts are mostly right (factual recall) or mostly wrong (trick items).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate: Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
finding: Large benchmark: 5 debate methods x 9 benchmarks x 4 models. Debate usually fails to beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency, even with far more compute.
numbers: Per-config ANOVA over 36 configs (4 models x 9 datasets): SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cases; Multi-Persona had 0% win rate. With GPT-4o-mini, SoM below CoT on all 9 datasets. Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: only AgentVerse above CoT (+0.85%); others at least -3.60%.
limits: Debate did better on math than on programming. EoT reproduced its GSM8K and CSQA gains.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of broad debate claims. Keep a CoT plus sampling baseline.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate: Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
finding: Self-consistency scales with extra tokens; debate does not. Debate both corrects and breaks answers: aggressive methods break many right answers, conservative ones fix few.
numbers: Multi-Persona, ChatEval and AgentVerse corrected many wrong answers but also altered many initially correct ones; SoM and EoT were conservative with fewer errors and fewer fixes (Fig 4, Fig 6).
limits: Counts in figures only.
agent_relevance: Premature agreement versus stubbornness is a trade-off: the right design needs both detection of errors and protection of correct answers.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate: Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
finding: Model heterogeneity helps debate: mixing two different models beat the per-model averages.
numbers: Heter-SoM +6.4% over SoM-average; Heter-EoT +8.2% over EoT-average; all heterogeneous MAD beat CoT-average by up to 5.8%. Gains smaller for ChatEval and AgentVerse.
limits: Only two-model mixes, from the position paper's own experiment. Contrasts with Wynn et al, where a weaker model hurt.
agent_relevance: Diverse errors help; correlated errors from one model repeat. Fits sampling independent drafts with different prompts or models.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (demonstration plus detailed question description) matches the best multi-agent discussion. Discussion only wins when there is no demonstration.
numbers: FOLIO-wiki, GSM8K, ECQA etc.; frameworks MAD, Debate, CMD, ReConcile. Debate and CMD got worse on ECQA when demonstrations were added.
limits: Gaps are small; named frameworks only; results with no demo still favour discussion.
agent_relevance: Prompt quality may substitute for discussion. Spend effort on the first draft prompt before adding exchange.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: Most common discussion error is wrong answer propagation: an agent drops its correct answer and adopts an incorrect consensus, even when most initial answers were right. A second error is judge mistake in ties.
numbers: Case study on FOLIO-wiki; described as the most common mistake in discussion. No frequency table in text.
limits: Qualitative case study.
agent_relevance: Matches human premature consensus. A judge or tie-break needs evidence, not preference for fluent text.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: The founding positive result: debate beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on arithmetic, GSM8K and chess.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds. Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9. Gains grew with agents; more than 4 rounds gave similar results.
limits: ChatGPT-3.5 era; small test sets with wide error bars (GSM8K debate 85.0 +/- 3.5 vs majority 81.0 +/- 3.9 overlap). Later work (b05, b08, b10) finds majority vote about equals debate.
agent_relevance: The claim that later work tests. Early positive results had overlapping intervals on GSM8K.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Debates converge to one answer that need not be correct; agents then confidently affirm it. Agents with high shared confidence resist persuasion.
numbers: Authors report converged but wrong answers; ease of persuasion suggested as a gauge of factual confidence. Long debates: models focus on latest turns.
limits: Observation, no rate given.
agent_relevance: Consensus is not evidence of truth. Do not treat agreement as a verification signal.

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Defines disagreement collapse rate (DCR). DCR is high in decentralized debate and falls with a judge.
numbers: Llama3.3-70B homogeneous 2-agent decentralized CSQA: DCR 86.36%. Qwen-Qwen CSQA decentralized 83.62 (DCR 81.71) vs single 85.50; with a judge 86.65 (DCR 41.27). MMLU Pro Qwen-Qwen: single 66.46, decentralized 66.60, centralized 71.10.
limits: Qwen3-32B and Llama3.3-70B, 2 and 3 agents, two datasets.
agent_relevance: A judge cut collapse by half in 2-agent debate. Direct support for an adjudicator that is separate from the debaters.

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: More agents and a moderate sycophancy mix matter. Three-agent debates collapse less and are more accurate than two-agent ones. Best settings mix peacemaker and troublemaker roles; all-peacemaker is worst.
numbers: CSQA homogeneous Qwen 2-agent accuracy 81.98 to 83.87 across 45 persona configs, lowest when both are peacemakers. Heterogeneous Qwen-Llama: 78.95 to 82.06 across 81 configs, best when both are troublemakers. 3-agent decentralized MMLU Pro Qwen-Qwen-Qwen 72.10 (DCR 31.66) vs single 66.46.
limits: Persona effects small (about 2 to 3 points) in homogeneous debates.
agent_relevance: Assigned dissent roles help modestly. Tune dissent level; do not maximise it.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Conformity in Large Language Models (ACL)
finding: Asch-style test on LLMs: all tested models conform to a unanimous wrong majority. Conformity rises with number of confederates and when the model is less confident.
numbers: Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen2-7B (instruct); 2 to 10 participants; MMLU, BBH, PopQA, CSQA, Politiscale, OpinionsQA. Resistance falls and conformity grows as confederates grow. Questions never conformed to had higher initial confidence (logprob; EigV).
limits: Prompted text majority, not real interactive agents. Small open models.
agent_relevance: Confidence is a predictor of resisting the crowd: low-confidence drafts should be protected from, or sent through, checks before accepting consensus.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Conformity in Large Language Models (ACL)
finding: Instruction tuning lowers conformity; more natural wording of the majority raises it. Devil's Advocate (one dissenter) and Question Distillation reduce conformity.
numbers: TriviaQA sycophancy, Llama-3-8B base: sycophantic 63.20%, correct 36.80%; with Devil's Advocate sycophantic 41.37%, correct 57.82%. Instruct: sycophantic 25.18% to 12.37%, correct 74.82% to 87.62%. DA also helped Gemma2 and Llama3 on MMLU, less on Mistral and Qwen2.
limits: Even an incorrect dissenter reduced conformity. DA worked on subjective items, unlike Allen & Levine (1969) human findings.
agent_relevance: One dissenting voice, even wrong, helps a draft resist consensus. Candidate for a devil's advocate operator.

source: Xiong et al. (2023) Examining Inter-Consistency of LLMs Collaboration: An In-depth Analysis via Debate
finding: Two LLMs with comparable ability can reach a shared goal, but with mismatched ability the stronger one dominates and the weaker one compromises; a stubborn weaker model can distract the stronger and lower total performance.
numbers: Six LLMs (ChatGPT, GPT-4, text-davinci-003 and open 13B models), COPA, e-CARE, Social IQa, PIQA, StrategyQA; FORD framework with judge.
limits: Pre-2024 models; table numbers not extracted here (summary conclusions only).
agent_relevance: Disagreement resolved by compromise, not by evidence, so error can win.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate (EMNLP)
finding: Self-reflection shows Degeneration of Thought: once confident, the model cannot generate new thoughts. Debate with a moderate tit-for-tat stance helps; forcing disagreement on every point is not best.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic: GPT-3.5 26.0, +CoT 28.0, +Self-Consistency 29.5, +Self-Reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0, GPT-4 51.0. Must-disagree-on-every-point prompt (disagreement 0.988) was not best. More debaters reduced performance in their tests (Table 7).
limits: 200-question set; judge shows bias toward same-model side; long-context limits.
agent_relevance: Dissent has an optimum: some, not total. Supports bounded devil's advocate rather than adversarial default.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy built from 150 traces and 1600+ annotated traces across 7 open-source multi-agent systems; failure rate 41% to 86.7%. Failure classes include premature termination, ignoring other agents' input, incomplete or incorrect verification.
numbers: Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 systems; MAST-guided prompt fix gave +9.4% task success for ChatDev with the same model; over 20 hours annotation per expert for the first 150 traces.
limits: Task-completion failures, not accuracy of QA debate; per-mode percentages not extracted from the garbled figure.
agent_relevance: Verification gaps and premature stopping are major causes. Supports an explicit check step before any consensus is accepted.

source: Franzen & Mader (2023) The power of social influence: A replication and extension of the Asch experiment
finding: Modern Asch replication with 5 confederates reproduced the classic error rate, and a small incentive cut it.
numbers: N=202 analysed (210 recruited). Error rate 33% non-incentivised vs Asch 36.8% (t(16)=0.59, p=0.57). With 1 CHF per correct answer: 25%. Mean wrong answers over 6 critical trials 1.97 vs 1.47 (t(208)=2.24, p=0.03). Political opinion statements: mean conformity 38%. Only Openness correlated negatively with conformity; intelligence and self-esteem no effect.
limits: Swiss students, face to face, strangers; small incentive; no dissenter condition; share conforming at least once not reported. Read via WebFetch summary of the page.
agent_relevance: Conformity pressure replicates after 70 years, and rewards for accuracy reduce it (human analogue of the correctness payoff; compare b04 where the LLM payoff prompt did not).

source: Lu, Yuan, McLeod (2012) Twenty-Five Years of Hidden Profiles in Group Decision Making: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Groups discuss shared information much more than unshared information, and hidden-profile groups rarely find the best option.
numbers: 65 studies, 101 independent effects, 3,189 groups. Groups mentioned about two SD more common than unique information. Hidden profile groups were eight times less likely to find the solution than full-information groups. Information coverage predicted decision quality more than discussion focus. Moderators: group size, total information load, proportion unique, task demonstrability, hidden profile strength. Medium had no effect.
limits: Abstract only (via Crossref); publisher page blocked (403).
agent_relevance: Core human evidence for premature agreement on shared knowledge. Agent analogue: drafts should list what only one sample knows before agreeing.

source: Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt (2010) Knowing others' preferences degrades the quality of group decisions (JPSP)
finding: Learning others' preferences before discussion hurts solving hidden profiles. Four experiments, replicated in face-to-face three-person groups.
numbers: Experiments 1-3: participants not told others' preferences solved hidden profiles more often than those given bogus preference information. Effect mediated by less attention to exchanged information; not due to defending own position or information load. Held when one member favored the correct option. Exp 4: 3-person face-to-face. Sample sizes not on the page.
limits: Abstract-level summary only; sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Direct design lesson: write your own answer before seeing peers' answers (independent first pass).

source: Schulz-Hardt, Brodbeck, Mojzisch, Kerschreiter, Frey (2006) Group decision making in hidden profile situations: Dissent as a facilitator for decision quality (JPSP)
finding: Title only (311 citations). Title claim: dissent facilitates decision quality in hidden profile groups.
numbers: No numbers read; abstract not available via Crossref or PubMed in this session.
limits: Not opened. Do not use any numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Supports dissent before discussion; verify with the paper before relying on effect sizes.

source: Reimer, Reimer, Czienskowski (2010) Decision-Making Groups Attenuate the Discussion Bias in Favor of Shared Information: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Title only: decision-making groups attenuate the shared-information discussion bias. Possible boundary condition to Lu et al.
numbers: No numbers read; Crossref abstract missing.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Boundary: when groups know they must decide, the bias may shrink. Task framing may matter; verify.

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect (PNAS)
finding: Mild social influence narrows diversity of estimates without improving collective accuracy, pushes truth to the edge of the range, and raises confidence.
numbers: N=144, five estimation rounds, three conditions (no info, average info, full info). Three effects named: social influence, range reduction, confidence.
limits: Abstract only (PMC record front matter); topic covered in sibling subfield 04.
agent_relevance: Sharing others' answers before commit reduces diversity with no accuracy gain.

source: Park (1990) and later reviews of empirical groupthink studies, via Wikipedia Groupthink article
finding: Empirical tests give only partial support to Janis. Cohesiveness has no reliable main effect. Homogeneity and insulation do better.
numbers: Park (1990): 16 empirical studies; fewer than two dozen between 1972 and 1998 (Turner & Pratkanis). Cohesion non-significant in Fodor & Smith (1982) and Leana (1985); structural conditions predicted groupthink in McCauley (1989); Choi & Kim (1999): groupthink to defective decisions insignificant. Baron (2005): Janis's antecedents neither necessary nor reliably amplifying.
limits: Secondary source (Wikipedia); no formal meta-analysis on the page. Kramer (1998) disputes Janis's Bay of Pigs reading.
agent_relevance: Do not build the agent around Janis's cohesion story. The sturdier lever is process: independent input, structured dissent, outside views.

source: Hartwig (2007), Sunstein, Hong & Page (2004) remedies, via Wikipedia Groupthink article
finding: Remedies named: critical evaluator role, leaders withhold opinions, independent parallel groups, outside experts, rotating devil's advocate. Sincere dissent is said to beat role-played dissent.
numbers: Hartwig (2007): devil's advocacy useful for structured problem solving. Hong & Page (2004): diverse team beat team of top individuals. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: Secondary summary. Nemeth's authentic-dissent work not checked in this session.
agent_relevance: Role-played dissent may be weaker than genuine independent drafts. For an agent, independently sampled drafts are the closest to authentic dissent, with the caveat that they share one model's bias.
